# Auto Ontology

Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.

It enables developers to:

- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API.
Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.

## Benchmarks

To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the
[ontology SQL evaluation repository](https://github.com/NVIDIA/ontology-sql-eval/).

> **Licensing & contributions.** Auto Ontology is distributed under the
> [Apache License 2.0](./LICENSE). Third-party open-source components
> bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
> [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](./THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). **This project
> is currently not accepting external contributions.**

<p>
<img src="./docs/assets/arch.png" alt="Auto Ontology Architecture" width="800">
</p>

## Key Features

- **Natural-language querying** of structured data — questions are translated to
  SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
- **Semantic catalog / ontology layer** over relational sources, stored in
  Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
- **Authentication & RBAC** —using [Better Auth](https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth).
- **Web UI** for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
- **Flexible deployment** — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a
  local stack.

## Software Components

| Component           | Technology                                                             | Role                                       | Default port |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------ |
| Frontend            | Next.js 16 (React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4), Better Auth, Prisma | Web UI, authentication, API gateway        | 3000         |
| Backend             | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain                                      | Chat / NL-to-SQL, catalog, datasource APIs | 3001         |
| Ingestion worker    | FastAPI (Python 3.12+)                                                 | Ingests tabular data and writes embeddings | 3002         |
| Postgres + pgvector | Relational Database                                                    | App metadata, the catalog and ontology, vector store | 5432 |
| HashiCorp Vault     | Optional                                                               | Secure storage of connection credentials   | —            |

### NVIDIA NIM

Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
[NVIDIA API catalog](https://build.nvidia.com) (`integrate.api.nvidia.com`) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in `.env.example` are:

- **LLM:** `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b`
- **Embeddings:** `nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b`
- **Reranking:** `nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2`

The endpoints and models are configured via the `DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT`, `DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL`,
`EMBED_ENDPOINT`, and `EMBED_MODEL` environment variables and require a
`DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`.

#### Model triplets

Each model role is configured by a **triplet** of environment variables —
`<PREFIX>_ENDPOINT` (URL), `<PREFIX>_API_KEY`, and `<PREFIX>_MODEL`:

| Prefix           | Role                                                        |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEFAULT_MODELS` | Shared default; every field below falls back to it.         |
| `REASONING`      | Main chat / NL-to-SQL model.                                |
| `NON_REASONING`  | Lighter model used for entity extraction.                   |
| `EMBED`          | Text-embedding model (must match between ingest and query). |
| `RERANK`         | Reranker used by the retrieval flow.                        |

You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching `DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>`. So the simplest
setup is to fill in `DEFAULT_MODELS_*` and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. `EMBED_MODEL`, `NON_REASONING_MODEL`). `*_API_KEY` also falls
back to the legacy `NVIDIA_API_KEY` for backward compatibility.

## Quickstart

This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and an NVIDIA API key (`nvapi-...`) from
[build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com).

1. Clone the repository and create `.env`:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology
   cp .env.example .env
   ```

   Then set these values in `.env`:

   ```dotenv
   DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-...
   AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32>
   APP_URL=http://localhost:3000
   POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters
   AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password>
   ```

   Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
   each default password before you start it. `.env.example` also sets an API
   key per model role: replace each `nvapi-your-api-key-here` with your key, or
   delete those lines so they fall back to `DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY`.

2. Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in
   auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --wait postgres
   git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval
   (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \
     POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \
     uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)
   ```

3. Build and start the rest of the stack:

   ```bash
   docker compose up -d --build
   ```

4. Open <http://localhost:3000> and sign in with `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL` and
   `AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD` from `.env`. Go to **Settings → Semantic
   Compilation** and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
   immediately and reports **Semantic compilation is ready** when it finishes.

5. Ask a question in **Chat**:

   > What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania
   > in June 2015?

   The agent resolves *revenue*, *product*, and *state* to terms in the
   ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the
   query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it,
   so you can check the result against the source:

   ```text
   Answer:  Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
            June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.

   SQL:     SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
            FROM sales.invoicelines il
            JOIN sales.invoices i             ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
            JOIN warehouse.stockitems si      ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
            JOIN sales.customers c            ON i.customerid = c.customerid
            JOIN application.cities ct        ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
            JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
            WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
              AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
              AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'

   Steps:   Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
            Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
            Validated the filter values against the data, then executed
   ```

6. Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no
   advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve
   against. An agent connected through [MCP](#mcp-server) checks answerability
   first and asks you to clarify:

   ```text
   You:    What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
   Agent:  check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
   Agent:  I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
           advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
           want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
           source I should connect?
   ```

If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for `localhost:3000` and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
[setup skill's troubleshooting guide](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/references/troubleshooting.md).

## How it works

<p>
<img src="./docs/assets/arch.png" alt="Auto-Ontology architecture" width="800">
</p>

Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify
it, and the agent answers questions from it.

The ontology holds three kinds of definition:

- **Terms.** Business concepts such as *Customer* or *Invoice Line*, each with a
  description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.
- **SQL attributes.** Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or
  a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the
  same way.
- **Relationships.** How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from
  keys and from the data.

**Generate.** The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source
databases:

1. Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the
   catalog.
2. Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.
3. Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and
   suggest SQL attributes from query history.
4. Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in
   Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.

The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one
compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting **Order** shows
its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:

<p>
<img src="./docs/assets/ontology-graph.png" alt="Semantic graph of the Wide World Importers ontology, with the Order term selected" width="800">
</p>

**Certify.** People make the draft trustworthy:

1. Test with real questions in Chat, or with `check_answerable` and
   `ask_question` over MCP.
2. Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.
3. Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.

**Answer.** For each question, the agent:

1. Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.
2. Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.
3. Writes SQL from those candidates.
4. Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the
   SQL when a check fails.
5. Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.

When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question
can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's
configured (see [Predictions](#predictions)).

In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as
CSV, or read them as a chart:

<p>
<img src="./docs/assets/qa-example.png" alt="Chat answering which products drive the most revenue and highest customer count, with the generated SQL and a revenue chart" width="550">
</p>

Auto-Ontology is compatible with [Apache Ossie](https://ossie.apache.org/), the
open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a
[converter for Auto-Ontology](https://github.com/apache/ossie-converters/tree/main/nvidia),
which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML.
Use **Settings → Import / Export**, or `POST /api/model/import` and
`POST /api/model/export`.

| Component           | Technology                        | Role                                       | Port |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| Frontend            | Next.js, Better Auth, Prisma      | Web UI, authentication, public API gateway | 3000 |
| Backend             | FastAPI (Python 3.12+), LangChain | Text-to-SQL agent, catalog, ontology APIs  | 3001 |
| Ingestion service   | FastAPI (Python 3.12+)            | Ingestion and semantic compilation         | 3002 |
| MCP server          | FastMCP                           | Read-only agent tools over the public API  | 3003 |
| Postgres + pgvector | PostgreSQL 17                     | Catalog, ontology, app data, vector store  | 5432 |
| HashiCorp Vault     | Optional                          | Connection credential storage              | n/a  |

Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity
the frontend forwards in the `x-auto-ontology-user-id` header, and the ingestion
service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of
their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000.

## Use it from your agent

### MCP server

The [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server gives any MCP client read-only
tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every
call runs with that user's permissions.

| Job           | Tools                                                         |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Readiness     | `check_readiness`: can this deployment answer anything at all |
| Terms         | `search_terms`, `get_term`, `get_term_columns`, `get_term_sql_attributes`, `get_sql_attribute`, `describe_table` |
| Answerability | `check_answerable`: does the ontology cover this question     |
| Questions     | `ask_question`: the answer, the SQL, and the rows             |

Run the server against your deployment:

```bash
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
  uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp
```

Cursor (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" }
  }
}
```

Claude Desktop (`claude_desktop_config.json`), bridged with
[`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["mcp-remote", "http://localhost:3003/mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts.
Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in [docs/mcp.md](./docs/mcp.md).

### Agent skills

Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at
[AGENTS.md](./AGENTS.md).

| Skill                                                                | Covers                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| [`nvidia-ontology-setup`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-setup/)           | Install, connect sources, compile, prove readiness   |
| [`nvidia-ontology-management`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-management/) | Inspect, model, certify, import/export, and publish  |
| [`nvidia-ontology-query`](./skills/nvidia-ontology-query/)           | Ask questions and validate the SQL, rows, and answer |

### REST API

Ask a question with `POST /api/chat/completions` on the web app's origin. Mint
an API token under the user menu → **API Tokens**. The response is a
server-sent event stream: a `result` event carries the answer, and
`data: [DONE]` ends the stream.

```bash
curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \
  -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}'
```

```python
import json
import os

import requests

response = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions",
    headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]},
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
    stream=True,
    timeout=900,
)
response.raise_for_status()

for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
        continue
    payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip()
    if payload == "[DONE]":
        break
    event = json.loads(payload)
    if event["type"] == "result":
        print(event["answer"]["response"])
        print(event["answer"]["sql_code"])
    elif event["type"] == "error":
        raise RuntimeError(event["message"])
```

Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in
[docs/conversation-api.md](./docs/conversation-api.md). Every other operation is
in the [OpenAPI spec](./docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json).

## Connectors, models, and predictions

### Sources

Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines:

- PostgreSQL
- MySQL
- Databricks
- Snowflake
- ClickHouse
- Trino
- Apache Kyuubi
- HeavyDB
- DuckDB
- SQLite

Add connections under **Settings → Connections**, or list them in
`CONNECTION_STRINGS`. DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See
[docs/connections.md](./docs/connections.md) for URL schemes, scoping, and
credential storage.

### Models

Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an `nvapi-` key, each defaults to an
NVIDIA NIM on [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com):

| Role            | Default model                           | What it does                                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `REASONING`     | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Builds the ontology (terms, relationships, SQL attributes), writes each answer's SQL and explanation, and grades answerability |
| `NON_REASONING` | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b` | Runs the agent's faster steps: question intent, entity extraction, candidate selection, and SQL checks and repair              |
| `EMBED`         | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-embed-1b`          | Indexes tables, columns, terms, and SQL attributes in pgvector, and matches each question to them                              |
| `RERANK`        | `nvidia/nemotron-3.5-rerank-8b`         | Ranks candidate tables when compilation builds bridge-table SQL attributes                                                     |

<div align="center">
    <img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/github/spec-kit/main/media/logo_large.webp" alt="Spec Kit Logo" width="200" height="200"/>
    <h1>🌱 Spec Kit</h1>
    <h3><em>Build with a spec, fix a bug, or assess an idea — with your coding agent.</em></h3>
</div>

<p align="center">
    <a href="https://github.com/github/spec-kit/releases/latest"><img src="https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/github/spec-kit" alt="Latest Release"/></a>
    <a href="https://github.com/github/spec-kit/stargazers"><img src="https://img.shields.io/github/stars/github/spec-kit?style=social" alt="GitHub stars"/></a>

<p align="center">
    <strong>English</strong> ·
    <a href="./README.zh-CN.md">简体中文</a> ·

</p>

Spec Kit is an open source toolkit that gives AI coding agents structured
processes, reusable templates, and documented outcomes. Start with a ready-made
process, customize it, or bring your own.

## Choose your process

| What you need | Process | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Build a feature or application | [Spec-Driven Development](#spec-driven-development) | A specification carried through planning, implementation, and convergence |
| Diagnose and repair broken behavior | [Bug fixing](#bug-fixing) | An assessed cause, scoped fix, and recorded verification |
| Decide whether an idea deserves investment | [Idea assessment](#idea-assessment) | An evidence-backed go, clarify, or stop decision |
| Adopt or create a different process | [Your own process](#capabilities) | A process adapted or assembled from reusable primitives |

These are independent entry points, not mandatory phases. SDD ships in core;
bug fixing and assessment are bundled extensions you install when needed, and
the primitives below let you adopt or create other processes.

## Capabilities

Spec Kit combines ready-to-use processes with composable mechanisms:

| Capability | Spec Kit mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| Connect to or switch between coding agents | [Integration](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/index.html) |
| Add a command, quality gate, or complete process | [Extension](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/overview.html) |
| Connect a process to an external tool or service | [Extension](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/overview.html) |
| React to coding-agent lifecycle events | [Extension runtime event](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/api.html#extension-runtime-events) |
| Run extension commands before or after Spec Kit commands | [Extension hook](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/extensions/api.html#hook-configuration) |
| Adapt templates, commands, terminology, or methodology | [Preset](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/presets/overview.html) |
| Enforce organizational or regulatory standards | [Preset](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/presets/overview.html) |
| Override a template for one project | [Project-local override](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/customization.html#project-local-overrides-and-resolution) |
| Automate prompts, commands, gates, and shell tasks | [Workflow](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflows/overview.html) |
| Modify an installed workflow without forking it | [Workflow overlay](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflows/overlays.html) |
| Add reusable executable behavior to workflows | [Workflow step](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/workflow-steps/developing.html#custom-step-packages) |
| Install a curated setup for a role or team | [Bundle](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/bundles/overview.html) |
| Discover community components | [Catalog](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/catalogs.html) |
| Host a private catalog of approved components | [Catalog](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/catalogs.html) |
| Access private catalogs and component downloads | [Authentication](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/authentication.html) |
| Work offline or behind a firewall | [Local sources and self-hosted catalogs](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/install/air-gapped.html) |
| Inspect which layer supplies a command, template, or script | [Artifact inventory](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/overview/artifacts.html) |

Search the active catalogs with commands such as `specify extension search`,
`specify preset search`, `specify workflow search`, and `specify bundle search`.
Spec Kit includes community catalogs, and organizations can add their own
curated sources. Catalog listings are not audits or endorsements, so review
community source code before installing or running it.

<a id="-get-started"></a>
<a id="-prerequisites"></a>

## Get started

You need Python 3.11+, [uv](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/install/uv.html),
and a supported AI coding agent on Linux, macOS, or Windows.

Run these commands in your terminal to install Spec Kit and create a project.
This example uses GitHub Copilot.

```bash
uv tool install specify-cli
specify init my-project --integration copilot
cd my-project
```

<a id="-supported-ai-coding-agent-integrations"></a>

After installing the Specify CLI and creating your project, launch your coding
agent in the project directory, then choose a process below.

For other setups:

- [Installation](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/installation.html) for pinned releases, other installers, CI, and troubleshooting.
- [Existing projects](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/existing-projects.html) to start with code you already have.
- [Other agents](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/index.html) for integration keys and [invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation).
- [Upgrade](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/upgrade.html) to update an existing installation.

<a id="-what-is-spec-driven-development"></a>
<a id="sdd-quickstart"></a>

## Spec-Driven Development

Define what to build and why, then turn the specification into a plan, tasks,
and working code.

The minimal flow is shown below. Create a constitution once per project and
repeat the remaining steps for each feature. Run these skills in your agent's
chat, not your terminal, one at a time, reviewing each result before continuing.

This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent,
use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation).

```text
/speckit-constitution Create principles focused on code quality, testing, and maintainability.
/speckit-specify Build a photo organizer with albums grouped by date and a tile preview of each album.
/speckit-plan Use Vite with vanilla JavaScript. Keep images local and store metadata in SQLite.
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge
```

Repeat implement and converge until convergence reports `Converged`.
For clarification, checklists, and consistency analysis, see the SDD walkthrough.

[SDD walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/quickstart.html) ·
[Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-sdd.html)

<a id="-bug-fixing-with-spec-kit"></a>
<a id="bug-fix-quickstart"></a>

## Bug fixing

Assess the cause, fix the bug, and verify the original symptom is resolved.
No SDD feature workflow is required first.

Install the bug-fixing extension in your terminal, from the project directory:

```bash
specify extension add bug
```

Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time,
reviewing each result before continuing.

This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent,
use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation).

```text
/speckit-bug-assess "Submitting an empty password crashes the login form." slug=login-crash
/speckit-bug-fix slug=login-crash
/speckit-bug-test slug=login-crash
```

Review the reports in `.specify/bugs/login-crash/`. The final verdict is
`verified`, `partial`, or `failed`; only `verified` confirms a successful fix.

[Bug-fixing walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/guides/bugfix.html) ·
[Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-bugfix.html)

<a id="-assessing-ideas-with-spec-kit"></a>
<a id="idea-assessment-quickstart"></a>

## Idea assessment

Gather evidence to decide whether an idea is worth pursuing.
No source code or SDD feature workflow is required.

Install the assessment extension in your terminal, from the project directory:

```bash
specify extension add assess
```

Run these skills in your agent's chat, not your terminal, one at a time,
reviewing each result before continuing.

This example uses GitHub Copilot's default skills syntax. For another agent,
use its [equivalent invocation syntax](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/integrations/cli.html#command-invocation).

```text
/speckit-assess-intake "Let users work offline and sync when they reconnect." slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-research slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-define slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-shape slug=offline-mode
/speckit-assess-decide slug=offline-mode
```

Review the artifacts in `.specify/assessments/offline-mode/` and the final
decision: `go`, `needs-clarification`, or `kill`. Resolve unknowns by editing the
existing Markdown artifacts, directly or with your agent, rather than rerunning
whole stages. If you choose to build a software idea with a `go` decision,
establish a project constitution if needed, then pass the handoff summary from
`decision.md` to `/speckit-specify`. Stopping with a documented reason is also a
useful outcome.

[Assessment walkthrough](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/guides/assessment.html) ·
[Command reference](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/reference/agentic-assessment.html)

<a id="-making-spec-kit-your-own-extensions--presets"></a>
<a id="-bundles-role-based-setups"></a>
<a id="-community"></a>

## Customize or bring your own process

Customize Spec-Driven Development, bug fixing, or idea assessment to fit your
team's standards. Or bring your own process without adopting any of them.
Combine the [capabilities above](#capabilities) to match your goal:

- Adapt an existing process with a preset, such as requiring regulatory traceability in plans. Use a project-local override for a one-off template change.
- Bring your own process by adding its commands through an extension and exposing them to your coding agent through an integration.
- Automate commands and checks in a workflow. Use overlays to adapt an installed workflow without forking it, or add custom workflow steps when the built-in types are not enough.
- Share a reusable setup by packaging its extensions, presets, workflows, and workflow steps in a bundle.

Start with the smallest change that meets your needs; you do not have to replace
the whole process.

[Customization guide](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/how-to/customization.html) ·
[Community components and walkthroughs](https://github.github.io/spec-kit/community/overview.html)

 This repository contains the open-source PR Agent Project.

PR-Agent is an open-source, AI-powered code review agent and a community-maintained legacy project of Qodo. It is distinct from Qodo's primary AI code review offering, which provides a feature-rich, context-aware experience. Qodo offers a free version for open-source projects and integrates seamlessly with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps for high-quality automated reviews.

## Getting Started

> [!NOTE]
> **Docker Hub namespace migration.** Releases `0.34.2` and later are published under [`pragent/pr-agent`](https://hub.docker.com/r/pragent/pr-agent). Older releases (up to and including `v0.31`) remain available at the legacy [`codiumai/pr-agent`](https://hub.docker.com/r/codiumai/pr-agent) namespace as a frozen archive — no new images are pushed there. Update any pinned `image:` / `docker pull` / `uses: docker://` references when upgrading to `0.34.2+`.

### 🚀 Quick Start for PR-Agent

#### 1. GitHub Action (Recommended)

Add automated PR reviews to your repository with a simple workflow file:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/pr-agent.yml
name: PR Agent
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize]
jobs:
  pr_agent_job:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - name: PR Agent action step
      uses: the-pr-agent/pr-agent@main
      env:
        OPENAI_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_KEY }}
        GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```
[Full GitHub Action setup guide](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/installation/github/#run-as-a-github-action)

#### 2. CLI Usage (Local Development)

Run PR-Agent locally on your repository:

```bash
pip install "pr-agent[github]"
export OPENAI_KEY=your_key_here
pr-agent --pr_url https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/123 review
```
Git provider SDKs are optional extras: install the one for your provider ([list](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/installation/locally/#using-pip-package)), or `pr-agent[all]` for every integration.
[Complete CLI setup guide](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/usage-guide/automations_and_usage/#local-repo-cli)

- [Azure DevOps setup](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/installation/azure/)

## Why Use PR-Agent?

### 🎯 Built for Real Development Teams

**Fast & Affordable**: Each tool (`/review`, `/improve`, `/ask`) uses a single LLM call (~30 seconds, low cost)

**Handles Any PR Size**: Our [PR Compression strategy](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/core-abilities/compression_strategy/) effectively processes both small and large PRs

**Highly Customizable**: JSON-based prompting allows easy customization of review categories and behavior via [configuration files](pr_agent/settings/configuration.toml)

PR-Agent tools run as a comment on a PR or from the CLI. A few common ones:

```bash
# Comment on a PR (GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket/…):
/describe
/review
/improve
/ask "What does this PR change?" # free-text Q&A about the PR

# Issue-scoped commands run on an issue instead of a PR:
/similar_issue # find similar issues in the repository

# Or locally via the CLI:
pr-agent --pr_url <PR_URL> review
pr-agent --issue_url <ISSUE_URL> similar_issue
```

See the [Tools docs](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/tools/#usage-examples) for the full list of tools with example commands, and each tool's page for screenshots and options.

https://openai.com/enterprise-privacy

## Contributing

To contribute to the project, get started by reading our [Contributing Guide](https://github.com/the-pr-agent/pr-agent/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

For local verification, run `PYTHONPATH=. uv run pytest` from the repository root; it discovers the unit-test suite under `tests/unittest` by default. End-to-end tests under `tests/e2e_tests` require provider credentials and should be invoked explicitly, for example `PYTHONPATH=. uv run pytest tests/e2e_tests/test_github_app.py`.


## Big News for PR-Agent

PR-Agent has a new home!

After years of building this tool alongside the community, Qodo has donated PR-Agent to the open-source community - and we couldn't be more excited about what comes next.

The project now lives in the PR-Agent org on GitHub, is fully community-owned, and is open for contributions and additional maintainers.

What else changed:
- Docs moved to - [docs.pr-agent.ai](https://docs.pr-agent.ai/)
- Qodo Merge (Qodo 1.0), the hosted URL, which was the enterprise version of PR-Agent, has been rebranded and evolved into Qodo (Qodo 2.0), a full AI code review platform.

This open-source release remains here as a community contribution from Qodo — the origin of modern AI-powered code collaboration. We’re proud to share it and inspire developers worldwide.

The project now has its first external maintainer, Naor ([@naorpeled](https://github.com/naorpeled)), and is currently in the process of being donated to an open-source foundation.

Scrapling is a Python Web Scraping framework that brings fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, powerful parsing, and concurrent crawling into one library.

Scrape static pages, render JavaScript, interact with websites, and extract data from the API calls behind them. Build crawlers with reusable sessions, proxy rotation, automatic retries, pause/resume, and built-in data exports.

Use it from Python, the terminal, or your AI agent through its MCP server and Agent Skill. From extracting a few fields to collecting a whole website as clean Markdown, Scrapling covers the full scraping workflow.

## What you can do with Scrapling

- **[Fetch & interact](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/fetching/choosing.html)**: Fast HTTP requests, stealth browsers, JavaScript rendering, Cloudflare Turnstile/Interstitial handling, persistent sessions, and background API capture.
- **[Parse & extract](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/parsing/selection.html)**: CSS, XPath, text and regex search, adaptive element tracking, similar-element matching, and clean Markdown output.
- **[Crawl & export](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/spiders/getting-started.html)**: Concurrent spiders, proxy rotation, retries, AutoThrottle, pause/resume, streaming, ready-made templates, and JSON/JSONL/CSV/XML exports.
- **[Scrape with AI or from your terminal](https://scrapling.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ai/mcp-server.html)**: An MCP server for AI agents to browse and extract data, an Agent Skill, CLI commands, and an interactive shell.

Start with a single page:

```python
from scrapling.fetchers import Fetcher

page = Fetcher.get('https://quotes.toscrape.com/')
quotes = page.css('.quote .text::text').getall()
print(quotes)
```

Or scale up with a spider:

```python
from scrapling.spiders import Spider, Response

class QuotesSpider(Spider):
    name = "quotes"
    start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"]

    async def parse(self, response: Response):
        for quote in response.css('.quote'):
            yield {
                "text": quote.css('.text::text').get(),
                "author": quote.css('.author::text').get(),
            }

result = QuotesSpider().start()
print(len(result.items))
result.items.to_json("quotes.json")
```

This prints `10` and saves the quotes and authors to `quotes.json`.

## Why Horizon?

Good reads are scattered across feeds, forums, and timelines. Your attention isn't unlimited. Horizon collects, filters, and deduplicates them, then brings the worthwhile ones to you with context and community discussion.

Your taste shapes what you read—and what you want from it. A news story calls for “why it matters”; an engineering deep dive calls for “what I can use.” Horizon's **profiles** give each kind of content its own scoring criteria and output, for a briefing that feels handpicked.

## Features

- **📡 Bring Your Sources Together** — Follow RSS, Hacker News, Reddit, Telegram, X, GitHub, financial news, and more.
- **🎯 Decide What's Worth Reading** — Define scoring rubrics with profiles, set individual thresholds, and merge repeated stories within each profile.
- **🧩 Give Every Read the Right Treatment** — Choose summaries, context, solutions, or takeaways with Markdown prompts and JSON block definitions.
- **💬 Go Beyond the Headline** — Add web-researched background and community discussion where they help explain the story.
- **⚖️ Make Room for All Your Interests** — Cap the briefing's length and each category's share so one busy topic doesn't crowd out the rest.
- **📬 Read Where You Already Are** — Generate English and Chinese briefings as Markdown, publish to Pages, or deliver by email and webhook.

### One Briefing, Different Ways to Read

A profile is a reusable set of editorial rules: **what belongs, what's worth keeping, and what to write.** Built-in examples:

| What you follow | Profile | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| Technology news | `tech-news` | Events and context, with impact and community discussion when useful |
| Engineering deep dives | `tech-blog` | Background, solution, and practical takeaways |
| AI creator material | `ai-creator` | A summary, with timely hooks and content angles when useful |

Assign a profile to a source, or let AI choose. Want a different take? Adapt an existing profile—usually without changing Python. [Make a profile your own →](docs/profiles.md)

## How It Works

![Horizon architecture: ten sources feed a profile-driven pipeline with history and web search tools, delivering to Markdown, Pages, email, WeChat, and webhooks.](docs/assets/architecture.svg)

[Editable OmniGraffle source](docs/assets/architecture.graffle)

**Profiles define the treatment; runtime settings reflect your reading preferences.** Each item routes to one profile. Analysis, filtering, and deduplication happen before enrichment, then the selected items become a briefing grouped by profile.

Run the full pipeline through the CLI, or let an AI assistant call its stages through [MCP](src/mcp/README.md).

## Agent Skill

Let your AI assistant configure sources, customize Profiles, and run Horizon:

```bash
npx skills add Thysrael/Horizon --skill horizon -g
```

[Setup and usage](docs/agent-skill.md) · [Download Skill ZIP](https://thysrael.github.io/Horizon/downloads/horizon-skill.zip)

The command requires Node.js 22.20+. Then ask your assistant to install and configure Horizon, or follow the Quick Start below.

## Quick Start

### 1. Install

**Option A: Local Installation**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Thysrael/Horizon.git
cd Horizon

# Install with uv (recommended)
uv sync

# Install test/development extras when needed
uv sync --extra dev

# Or with pip
pip install -e .
```

`dev` is currently defined as an optional extra in `pyproject.toml`, so use `uv sync --extra dev` for pytest and other development dependencies.

If you want the optional OpenBB financial-news source, install its extra too:

```bash
uv sync --extra openbb
```

If `openbb` pulls packages without wheels on your machine, install the SDK manually with binaries only:

```bash
uv pip install --only-binary=:all: openbb openbb-benzinga
```

**Option B: Docker**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Thysrael/Horizon.git
cd Horizon

# Optional: build with comma-separated extras before the first run
docker compose build --build-arg EXTRAS=openbb horizon
```

Full-text extraction with `trafilatura` is included in the base install. The `twitter` extra also requires a Playwright browser and system packages, which the current Dockerfile does not install.

### 2. Configure

**Option A: Interactive wizard (recommended)**

```bash
uv run horizon-wizard
```

The wizard asks about your interests (e.g. "LLM inference", "嵌入式", "web security") and auto-generates `data/config.json`. See [Interactive Wizard](docs/configuration.md#interactive-wizard) for CLI options.

Eligible ChatGPT subscribers can choose `openai-chatgpt` to use their plan through [Sign in with ChatGPT](docs/chatgpt.md), without an OpenAI API key.

**Option B: Manual configuration**

```bash
cp .env.example .env          # Add your API keys
cp data/config.example.json data/config.json  # Customize your sources
```

Minimal manual configuration:

```jsonc
{
  "ai": {
    "provider": "openai",
    "model": "gpt-4",
    "api_key_env": "OPENAI_API_KEY"
  },
  "sources": {
    "rss": [
      {
        "name": "Simon Willison",
        "url": "https://simonwillison.net/atom/everything/",
        "profile": "tech-news"
      }
    ]
  },
  "processing": {
    "profiles_dir": "profiles",
    "default_profile": "tech-news",
    "profile_settings": {
      "tech-news": {
        "threshold": 7.0,
        "topic_dedup": true
      }
    }
  }
}
```

An explicit source `profile` uses that profile directly. Omit it or set it to
`"auto"` to let AI match the item against all available profiles. Set it to an
array such as `["tech-news", "finance-news"]` to restrict AI matching to those
profiles. See
[Processing Profiles](docs/profiles.md) for profile structure and behavior.
Per-profile user preferences such as score thresholds and topic deduplication
belong in `processing.profile_settings`, not in the profile files.

**Balanced digest (optional)**

Limit the final digest size and prevent one category from dominating the
results. Categories come from source configuration such as
`sources.rss[].category`.

```jsonc
{
  "digest": {
    "max_items": 20,
    "category_groups": {
      "ai": {
        "limit": 5,
        "categories": ["ai-news", "ai-tools", "machine-learning"]
      },
      "finance": {
        "limit": 5,
        "categories": ["finance", "business", "equities"]
      }
    },
    "default_group": "other",
    "default_group_limit": 3
  }
}
```

Group limits are applied after profile filtering and before enrichment. If
`category_groups`, `max_items`, and `default_group_limit` are omitted, no balanced
digest limits apply.

`api_key_env` must be the name of an environment variable, not the API key
itself. Put the real secret in `.env`:

```bash
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-your-key
```

For Gemini, use `GOOGLE_API_KEY`:

```jsonc
{
  "ai": {
    "provider": "gemini",
    "model": "gemini-2.0-flash",
    "api_key_env": "GOOGLE_API_KEY"
  }
}
```

Any string value in `data/config.json` can reference environment variables with `${VAR_NAME}`. This is useful for values such as `ai.base_url`, private RSS feed URLs, webhook endpoints, or custom header templates.

For the full reference, see the [Configuration Guide](docs/configuration.md).

### 3. Run

**A. Local installation**

```bash
uv run horizon [OPTIONS]
```

**B. Docker**

```bash
docker compose run --rm horizon [OPTIONS]
```

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `--hours N` | 24 | Fetch from last N hours |
| `-d`, `--data-dir PATH` | `data` | Path to the data directory |
| `-c`, `--config PATH` | `<data-dir>/config.json` | Path to config file |
| `-l`, `--log-level LEVEL` | `WARNING` | Logging level (DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR/CRITICAL) |

`--data-dir` changes the state directory, including summaries, subscribers, and the default config location; `--config` changes only the config file. The generated report is saved to `data/summaries/` (or `<data-dir>/summaries/` if `--data-dir` is set). See [Configuration Paths](docs/configuration.md#configuration-paths) for combining both flags and initializing a custom config location.

### 4. Automate (Optional)

Schedule Horizon with **GitHub Actions** using the [daily workflow template](.github/workflows/daily-summary.yml.disabled). The template is disabled in this repository; configure it for your deployment and rename it to `daily-summary.yml` to enable it.

Horizon can publish or deliver the generated briefing in several ways:

[GitHub release](https://github.com/scenario-labs/skills/releases), and posts the notes to the

Unlock datacenter-class intelligence on the hardware you already own — Run 290B+ frontier MoE models locally on your gaming PC at blistering interactive speeds.

## About

FreeToken is an edge-native Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) serving engine designed for running frontier-scale open-weight models on personal and consumer hardware. It treats heterogeneous edge resources—GPUs, CPUs, host memory, and interconnects—as a unified, elastic inference platform. Its core features include:  

- **Fast Edge-Native Runtime**: Provides efficient MoE serving with bandwidth-adaptive CPU–GPU co-execution ($q^\star$ policy), full-layer double-buffered prefill streaming, global LRU expert caching, graph-compatible execution, and the FTW fast weight format.  
- **Semantic-Aware Caching**: Features semantic anchor checkpoints for recurrent state and KV caches, allowing agentic context edits (e.g., tool calls, thinking blocks) to avoid redundant context recomputation.  
- **Elastic Memory Management**: Supports dynamic, runtime VRAM re-allocation between expert caches and KV memory without engine restarts or weight reloading.  
- **Broad MoE & Ecosystem Support**: Supports frontier open-weight MoE models (e.g., DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, GLM-5.2) across various parameter scales and quantization formats (e.g., MXFP4, NVFP4, FP8, BF16), with Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible APIs for seamless integration with real-world coding and tool-calling agents (e.g., Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw, DeepSeek Harness). 
- **Diverse Consumer Hardware**: Scales across consumer laptops, gaming desktops, and workstation GPUs, with native support for NVIDIA RTX 30, RTX 40, and RTX 50 series GPUs.  

## Getting Started

### Desktop app

Download FreeToken for Windows or Linux at [flashml.ai](https://www.flashml.ai/). It sets the engine up for you and gives you a GUI for running models, chatting, and tuning the engine.

<div align="center">

### CLI

Install FreeToken with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) (recommended) or pip:

```bash
uv pip install "freetoken[accel]"
```

Or build from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/FlashML-org/FreeToken.git && cd FreeToken
uv venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e ".[accel]"
```

</p>

---

## Start From A Video You Already Love

Starting from a reference video is often faster than starting from a blank prompt.

OpenMontage can start from a **YouTube video, Short, Reel, TikTok, or local clip** and turn it into a grounded production plan:

1. **Paste a reference video**
2. **The agent analyzes transcript, pacing, scenes, keyframes, and style**
3. **You get 2-3 differentiated concepts, an honest tool path, cost estimates, and a sample before full production**

```text
"Here's a YouTube Short I love. Make me something like this, but about quantum computing."
```

What you get back is not "best guess prompt spaghetti." You get:

- **What it keeps** from the reference: pacing, hook style, structure, tone
- **What it changes**: topic, visual treatment, angle, narration approach
- **What it will cost** at your target duration, before asset generation starts
- **What it will actually look like** with your currently available tools

Works with **Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, Codex** — any AI coding assistant that can read files and run code.

---

## Watch It Happen — The Backlot Living Storyboard

Chat tells you what the agent *said*. **Backlot shows you what the production is actually doing** — a local board that fills itself in as the pipeline runs. Stages light up, the script lands as a screenplay page, scene cards shimmer while assets generate, and every provider decision and dollar spent is on the wall.

When a production starts, the agent opens it for you automatically. No setup, no reporting — the board derives everything from the project files the pipeline already writes.

<p align="center"><img src="docs/images/backlot/board-live.png" alt="Backlot live board — assets generating" width="920"></p>

**The storyboard is now a real approval gate.** Asset generation pauses on a scene-by-scene contact sheet — takes, prompts, per-asset cost, quality scores — so you approve the visuals *before* the render, not after it's too late:

<p align="center"><img src="docs/images/backlot/storyboard.png" alt="Backlot storyboard — filmstrip with takes and renders" width="920"></p>

Creative gates hold until you answer. The board shows what's waiting and why; you reply in chat:

<p align="center"><img src="docs/images/backlot/script-gate.png" alt="Backlot script gate — awaiting approval" width="920"></p>

Every production on your machine, live-first, in the library:

<p align="center"><img src="docs/images/backlot/library.png" alt="Backlot library" width="920"></p>

```bash
python -m backlot open                  # the library — every project on disk
python -m backlot open <project-id>     # one production's live board
python scripts/backlot_simulate_run.py  # no production yet? watch a simulated one live
```

And when a run is done, hit **▶ REPLAY RUN** — the whole production replays from its timestamps, scrubbable end to end. See [`backlot/README.md`](backlot/README.md) for how it works.

---

## Quick Start

### Prerequisites

- **Python 3.10+** — [python.org](https://www.python.org/downloads/)
- **FFmpeg** — `brew install ffmpeg` / `sudo apt install ffmpeg` / [ffmpeg.org](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html)
- **Node.js 18+** — [nodejs.org](https://nodejs.org/)
- **An AI coding assistant** — Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot, Windsurf, or Codex

### Install & Run

```bash
git clone https://github.com/calesthio/OpenMontage.git
cd OpenMontage
make setup
```

Open the project in your AI coding assistant and tell it what you want:

```
"Make a 60-second animated explainer about how neural networks learn"
```

Or if you want the real-footage path:

```text
"Make a 75-second documentary montage about city life in the rain. Use real footage only, no narration, elegiac tone, with music."
```

That's it. The agent researches your topic with live web search, generates AI images, writes and narrates the script with voice direction, finds royalty-free background music automatically, burns in word-level subtitles, and renders the final video. Before you see anything, the system runs a multi-point self-review — ffprobe validation, frame sampling, audio level analysis, delivery promise verification, and subtitle checks. Every provider selection is scored across 7 dimensions with an auditable decision log. Every creative decision gets your approval.

> **No `make`?** macOS/Linux: `python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && python -m pip install -r requirements.txt && cd remotion-composer && npm install && cd .. && python -m pip install piper-tts && cp .env.example .env`
>
> Windows PowerShell: `py -3 -m venv .venv; .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1; python -m pip install -r requirements.txt; cd remotion-composer; npm install; cd ..; python -m pip install piper-tts; Copy-Item .env.example .env`
>
> **Windows:** If `npm install` fails with `ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE`, use `npx --yes npm install` instead.

### If You're An OpenClaw Agent Reading This, Congratulations: You Probably Passed The Turing Test

This repo is built for agentic operation. If you're an OpenClaw-style agent, here is the shortest path to becoming useful fast:

1. **Read the contract first**
   Start with [`AGENT_GUIDE.md`](AGENT_GUIDE.md), then [`PROJECT_CONTEXT.md`](PROJECT_CONTEXT.md).
2. **Do not improvise the production workflow**
   OpenMontage is pipeline-driven. Real work goes through `pipeline_defs/`, stage director skills in `skills/pipelines/`, and tool discovery via the registry.
3. **Check the actual capability envelope**
   Run:
   ```bash
   python -c "from tools.tool_registry import registry; import json; registry.discover(); print(json.dumps(registry.support_envelope(), indent=2))"
   python -c "from tools.tool_registry import registry; import json; registry.discover(); print(json.dumps(registry.provider_menu(), indent=2))"
   ```
4. **Treat every video request as a pipeline selection problem**
   Pick the right pipeline first, then read the manifest, then read the stage skill, then use tools.

### Add API Keys (optional — more keys = more tools)

```bash
# .env — every key is optional, add what you have

# Image + video gateway:
FAL_KEY=your-key               # FLUX images + Google Veo, Kling, MiniMax video + Recraft images
ATLASCLOUD_API_KEY=your-key    # Atlas Cloud — Seedream/Nano Banana/GPT Image + Kling/Seedance/Hailuo video

# Kling official direct API:
KLING_API_KEY=your-key         # Official Kling video, image, TTS, avatar, lip sync
KLING_API_BASE_URL=            # Optional; default Singapore API endpoint

# Free stock media:
PEXELS_API_KEY=your-key        # Free stock footage and images
PIXABAY_API_KEY=your-key       # Free stock footage and images
UNSPLASH_ACCESS_KEY=your-key   # Free stock images

# Music:
SUNO_API_KEY=your-key          # Full songs, instrumentals, any genre

# Voice & images:
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=your-key    # Premium TTS, AI music, sound effects
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key        # OpenAI TTS, GPT Image 2 images
XAI_API_KEY=your-key           # xAI Grok image edits/generation + Grok video generation
GOOGLE_API_KEY=your-key        # Google Imagen images, Google TTS (700+ voices)

# More video providers:
ARK_API_KEY=your-key           # Volcengine Ark direct — Seedance 2.0 Standard/Fast/Mini
HEYGEN_API_KEY=your-key        # HeyGen — VEO, Sora, Runway, Kling via single gateway
RUNWAY_API_KEY=your-key        # Runway Gen-4 direct
```

<details>
<summary><strong>Have a GPU? Unlock free local video generation</strong></summary>

```bash
make install-gpu

# Then add to .env:
VIDEO_GEN_LOCAL_ENABLED=true
VIDEO_GEN_LOCAL_MODEL=wan2.2-ti2v-5b  # or wan2.1-1.3b, wan2.1-14b, hunyuan-1.5, ltx2-local, cogvideo-5b
```

</details>

---

## What You Get With Zero API Keys

You don't need paid API keys to make real videos. Out of the box, `make setup` gives you:

| Capability | Free Tool | What It Does |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| **Narration** | Piper TTS | Free offline text-to-speech — real human-sounding narration |
| **Open footage** | Archive.org + NASA + Wikimedia Commons | Free/open archival footage, educational media, and documentary texture |

**Kornia** is a differentiable computer vision library that provides a rich set of differentiable image processing and geometric vision algorithms. Built on top of [PyTorch](https://pytorch.org), Kornia integrates seamlessly into existing AI workflows, allowing you to leverage powerful [batch transformations](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/gpu-acceleration.html), [auto-differentiation](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/differentiability.html) and [GPU acceleration](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/gpu-acceleration.html). Whether you're working on image transformations, augmentations, or AI-driven image processing, Kornia equips you with the tools you need to bring your ideas to life.

> **📢 Direction**: Kornia is becoming the **reference implementation and executable specification** for differentiable computer vision and geometry in the PyTorch ecosystem — explicit conventions, conformance tests, and honest benchmarks over API growth. Read the [Roadmap](ROADMAP.md).

## When to use Kornia

Kornia pays off where a hand-written version gets long or fragile, or where the alternatives leave the GPU:

- **Breadth.** 1,200+ public operators, most with no torchvision equivalent: camera models and
  epipolar geometry, minimal solvers and RANSAC, feature detection, description and matching, edge detection,
  morphology, Lab and Bayer color, image losses and metrics. torchvision overlaps mainly on resizing, cropping,
  flipping, color jitter and blur.
- **Per-sample parameters in one batched call.** `gaussian_blur2d(x, (9, 9), sigma)` takes a `(B, 2)` `sigma`;
  `rotate` takes a `(B,)` angle, `warp_affine` / `warp_perspective` take `(B, 2, 3)` / `(B, 3, 3)` matrices and
  `adjust_brightness` a `(B,)` factor. torchvision's functional ops apply one parameter per call. From Kornia 0.9.1,
  a `sigma` tensor and the enhancement value checks (gamma, contrast, solarize) are validated on the device, so a
  CUDA call, or an MPS call on PyTorch ≥ 2.13, needs no host synchronization for them.
- **Batched minimal solvers and robust estimation.** `find_fundamental(x1, x2, method="7POINT")` solves `(B, 7, 2)`
  samples and returns all real solutions in `(B, 3, 3, 3)`, with zero matrices in the unused slots; the 8-point,
  5-point essential (`find_essential`), DLT homography and PnP (`solve_pnp_dlt`) solvers are there too. `RANSAC`
  (homography, fundamental and essential models) samples and scores hypotheses on the device; by default its
  refinement and final selection run on the host in float64, and `compile=True` (PyTorch ≥ 2.14, CPU and CUDA) runs
  the whole estimation as one compiled graph on the device.
- **Differentiable geometry.** Depth to 3D and back (`depth_to_3d_v2`, `unproject_points`, `project_points`),
  `warp_frame_depth`, `remap`, camera models with Brown–Conrady and Kannala–Brandt distortion, and Lie groups (`So3`,
  `Se3`) keep gradients with respect to depth, pose and camera parameters.
- **Annotated augmentation.** `AugmentationSequential` applies one sampled transform to images, masks, boxes and
  keypoints together and can invert it, in 2D; the 3D augmentations transform volumes, without annotations or an
  inverse. On CUDA, augmentations move their sampled parameters to the
  GPU without blocking it, and a sync-guard test keeps every public augmentation free of avoidable host
  synchronizations.
- **Local features on the GPU.** SIFT and HardNet, DISK, ALIKED, XFeat, DeDoDe, LoFTR and LightGlue, with
  mutual-nearest-neighbour and ratio-test matchers.
- **Morphology** with arbitrary structuring elements on batched tensors.
- **Compiles and exports.** Nearly all probed operator configurations run under `torch.compile` and match eager,
  and over 1,000 export to ONNX; the result for every operator is on the
  [export support page](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/export-support.html).
- **Fast where it is designed to be: batched tensors on a GPU.** In the published 0.9.0 flagship benchmarks (RTX 4090,
  batch 32), many filters, warps, feature-matching steps and image metrics run about 10× to 70× faster in eager mode
  than per-image OpenCV or scikit-image on the CPU, and `torch.compile` takes several of them past 100×. On the small
  overlap with torchvision on the same GPU, eager Kornia is slower; compiled Kornia is faster for hue, color jitter
  and Gaussian blur and still slower for flips, crops and brightness. OpenCV wins single-image `uint8` CPU work.
  Results vary with hardware and workload; every number, win and loss is published on the
  [performance page](https://kornia.readthedocs.io/en/latest/get-started/performance.html).

These operators run on the input's device with no NumPy round trip, and most are differentiable; robust estimation
(`RANSAC`) and the extraction methods of learned features such as DeDoDe and XFeat run without gradients. For a
single fixed-parameter operation, such as one blur or one resize, a few lines of PyTorch or torchvision are just as
good.

## Key Components
1. **Differentiable Image Processing**<br>
  Kornia provides a comprehensive suite of image processing operators, all differentiable and ready to integrate into deep learning pipelines.
    - **Filters**: Gaussian, Sobel, Median, Box Blur, etc.
    - **Transformations**: Affine, Homography, Perspective, etc.
    - **Enhancements**: Histogram Equalization, CLAHE, Gamma Correction, etc.
    - **Edge Detection**: Canny, Laplacian, Sobel, etc.
    - ... check our [docs](https://kornia.readthedocs.io) for more.
2. **Advanced Augmentations**<br>
Perform powerful data augmentation with Kornia’s built-in functions, ideal for training AI models with complex augmentation pipelines.
    - **Augmentation Pipeline**: AugmentationSequential, PatchSequential, VideoSequential, etc.
    - **Automatic Augmentation**: AutoAugment, RandAugment, TrivialAugment.
3. **AI Models**<br>
Leverage pre-trained AI models optimized for a variety of vision tasks, all within the Kornia ecosystem.
    - **Face Detection**: YuNet
    - **Feature Matching**: LoFTR, LightGlue
    - **Feature Descriptor**: DISK, DeDoDe, SOLD2
    - **Segmentation**: SAM
    - **Classification**: MobileViT, VisionTransformer.

| **Image Processing**        | - Color conversions (RGB, Grayscale, HSV, etc.)<br>- Geometric transformations (Affine, Homography, Resizing, etc.)<br>- Filtering (Gaussian blur, Median blur, etc.)<br>- Edge detection (Sobel, Canny, etc.)<br>- Morphological operations (Erosion, Dilation, etc.)                                 |

# Open Duet

**Build a team of AI coworkers and choose where they run.**

Open Duet is an open-source workspace for creating named AI agents, giving
them jobs and workspaces, and bringing them together to complete tasks. Keep
useful context between conversations, run routines, and review actions before
they make changes. Use the desktop app, run your own server, or visit the
separate hosted service.

Open Duet does not include an AI model or model subscription. You choose the
engine and provider account used for your work.

## Project links

- [GitHub repository](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet)
- [Desktop downloads](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet/releases)
- [Hosted app](https://suparagent.ai)
- [Watch the demo](https://youtu.be/vtFy94DfETE)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Guides](#guides)
- [Discord support](https://discord.com/invite/zpnuBRXhKg)

<p align="center"><a href="https://youtu.be/vtFy94DfETE" title="Watch the Open Duet demo"><img src="https://i.ytimg.com/vi/vtFy94DfETE/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="Open Duet demo video thumbnail — click to watch on YouTube" width="720"></a></p>

> **Status:** Open Duet is in active development. Desktop releases, self-hosting,
> agent computers, and newer team features are still evolving. Review
> [known limitations](#known-limitations) before relying on them for important work.

## Contents

- [What you can do](#what-you-can-do)

## What you can do

- **Create agents and teams.** Give agents a name, role, engine, workspace,
  memory, and approval settings. A lead can delegate work to specialists or
  coordinate agents in shared rooms. Team leads can use Claude or Codex. See
  [teams and delegated work](docs/TEAMS.md).
- **Keep useful context.** Agents can save notes, recall relevant notes and
  conversations, and search their history. You can review and edit what they
  remember. See [memory](docs/MEMORY.md).
- **Run work on a schedule.** Create routines for scheduled, webhook, or manual
  runs. Review each result and answer requests for approval; a routine never
  approves an action by itself. See [routines](docs/ROUTINES.md).
- **Choose how much freedom agents have.** Use Ask first, Accept edits, Approve
  for me (Claude, Codex, and Cursor), or Plan only. Review tool activity and approval
  decisions in the app.
- **Connect tools and apps.** Connect services such as GitHub, Gmail, and Google
  Calendar through your own Composio key, then grant access to selected Claude
  or Codex agents. Changes wait for your approval. Add individual tools from
  the MCP Marketplace. See [connected apps](docs/CONNECTED_APPS.md).
- **See what needs your attention.** The Today view gathers approvals,
  questions, routine outcomes, engine failures, and due tasks. It can show
  read-only Gmail and calendar items. See [everyday features](docs/EVERYDAY.md).
- **Plan and follow work.** Use a task board and calendar to assign work,
  schedule one-time runs, and review conversations and attempts. See
  [tasks and calendar](docs/TASKS.md).
- **Reuse instructions.** Save skills and start agents from templates. Skills
  are instructions you choose for a message. See [skills](docs/SKILLS.md) and
  [templates](docs/TEMPLATES.md).
- **Use it from your phone.** Pair the phone app with your own server to chat,
  stop an answer, allow or deny a tool call, or create and edit agents and rooms.
  See the [phone app guide](docs/MOBILE.md).
- **Work with files and history.** Search conversations, attach text and
  images, import audio for transcription with your consent and credentials,
  browse or download workspace files, and export your history.

## Ways to run Open Duet

| | Desktop app | Self-hosted server | Hosted web app | Development checkout |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Best for | A personal workspace on your computer | Keeping your agents and routines available on a server you control | Using the separately operated Suparagent service | Contributing or changing Open Duet |
| Where workspace data lives | Your computer | Your server | An account-specific hosted workspace | Your development machine or configured database |
| Start here | [Quick start](#quick-start) | [Self-hosting guide](docs/SELF-HOSTING.md) | [suparagent.ai](https://suparagent.ai) | [Development setup](docs/SETUP.md) |
| Main requirements | Node.js 22+, uv, and an engine | Linux server, HTTPS, Docker or Node.js and uv, and an engine | An account and an AI provider account | Node.js, uv, and Docker if you use PostgreSQL |
| Status | Experimental | Experimental; single owner | Separate hosted product | — |

The hosted service is separate from the open-source desktop and self-hosted
core. Hosted account, workspace, and billing data are handled by Suparagent;
see the hosted service's [Privacy Policy](https://suparagent.ai/privacy) and
[Terms](https://suparagent.ai/terms).

## Hosted plans

The hosted preview lets you use your own Boat key for sandbox compute. Paid
plans use compute operated by Suparagent, so you do not need to supply a Boat
key. In both cases, you bring your AI provider account and pay that provider
for model usage.

| Plan | Monthly Suparagent price | Included running compute | Machine disk capacity |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Free preview | $0 | Billed to your Boat account | Small profile |
| Starter | $15 | 100 hours per billing period | 51 GB |
| Standard | $49 | 300 hours per billing period | 51 GB |
| Pro | $99 | 720 hours per billing period | 111 GB |

Paid-plan compute hours count while the sandbox is running, including idle
time. At the limit, it stops until the next billing period or a plan change;
compute overages are not charged. The disk value is the selected machine's
capacity, not a separate storage quota. A stopped sandbox's disk is subject to
the provider's retention period, so export important files before a paid plan
ends. Paid checkout is enabled for hosted accounts; see the
[Suparagent pricing page](https://suparagent.ai/pricing/) for current plans.

## Engines, data, and costs

Connect an engine you already use: Claude Code or Codex CLI, Gemini CLI,
Google Gemini through Antigravity, Cursor, another command-line agent using
the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), OpenRouter, or an OpenAI-compatible API such
as Ollama or LM Studio. Available tools vary by engine; image input and agent
computers, for example, are not supported by every engine. See
[engine setup and capabilities](docs/ENGINES.md).

For desktop and self-hosted use, conversations, agent notes, routines, and
settings are stored in that instance's local data folder or server database.
Workspace files stay in the folders you assign to agents. API keys saved
through Open Duet are encrypted there; command-line sign-ins remain with the
engine installed on that machine.

When an agent answers, the selected engine receives the prompt and the context
needed for that turn. This can include text you attach, relevant notes, and
workspace content the engine reads. If the engine is a hosted service, that
information is handled under that provider's terms. You bring the provider
account, CLI sign-in, or API key; model usage may cost money.

## Quick start

The desktop app runs from a source checkout. It needs Node.js 22 or newer,
[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and at least one engine available on the
same computer. For a CLI engine, install it and sign in before opening Open
Duet. You can also configure an API-based engine in **Settings → Engines**.
Docker is only needed for the optional isolated agent computers.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet.git
cd open-duet/desktop
npm run app
```

On first launch, choose an engine, workspace, and approval mode. Then:

1. Open **Settings → Engines** and confirm an engine is ready.
2. Create an agent with a name, a clear job, and a workspace.
3. Start a chat. Choose **Ask first** to pause for approval before actions that
   need it.
4. Add teammates or create a routine when you want to split up or repeat work.

See the [Releases page](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet/releases) for
current desktop installers and the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md) for changes.
Installers are experimental and unsigned. The assisted update flow offers a
SHA-256-verified installer for you to open; it does not install updates
automatically. The release-to-release update path has not been verified end to
end.

## Example: prepare a weekly project briefing

Create a lead agent and specialists, such as a researcher and an editor. Give
them the same project workspace, and set the lead's engine to Claude or
Codex. Ask the lead to prepare a briefing from the notes and reports in that
folder.

The lead can split the request into smaller tasks and hand them to the
specialists. Their work runs in separate conversations, then returns to the
lead to assemble. Follow along in chat and approve actions when the settings
require it. Once the process works well, make it a weekly routine and review
each run in the app.

## Scheduling tasks

Routines run prompts on local agents on a schedule, by webhook, or on demand.
They run in the backend, so the backend must stay running. The original
Telegram bot and [Boat](https://docs.boat.dev/api-keys) sandbox task flow are
optional and separate from the agent workspace. See [backend scheduling
details](backend/README.md#scheduling) and [environment settings](backend/.env.example).

## Known limitations

- Open Duet is early and changing. The self-hosted server is experimental and
  intended for one owner with paired devices, not a multi-user organization.
- Team delegation is new; lead agents need to use Claude or Codex.
- The phone app has been tried on an Android emulator and an Android phone, not
  on iOS. It has no push notifications or store release.
- Docker computers, browser tools, and the macOS native desktop preview are
  experimental and opt-in.
- Desktop installers are unsigned and have limited platform verification. See
  [desktop setup details](docs/SETUP.md#desktop-app-from-a-source-checkout-experimental).
- Connected apps are reached through Composio and tested against a fake
  Composio service, not yet the real service. Only Claude and Codex agents can
  use them, and changes wait for your approval.
- The MCP Marketplace, hosted cloud computers, quiet routine results, and
  audio transcription have not had live-service or packaged-app qualification.

## Guides

**Getting started**

- [First-run setup and approvals](docs/SETUP.md)
- [Engines and models](docs/ENGINES.md)
- [Self-hosting](docs/SELF-HOSTING.md)

**Agents and work**

- [Teams and delegated work](docs/TEAMS.md)
- [Agent settings and chat management](docs/CHAT_MANAGEMENT.md)
- [Memory and context](docs/MEMORY.md)
- [Routines](docs/ROUTINES.md)
- [Tasks and calendar](docs/TASKS.md)
- [Everyday features](docs/EVERYDAY.md): search, attachments, audio, and Today

**Tools and customization**

- [Connected apps](docs/CONNECTED_APPS.md)
- [App language settings](docs/LOCALIZATION.md)
- [Skills](docs/SKILLS.md) and [templates](docs/TEMPLATES.md)
- [Agent computers](docs/COMPUTERS.md), [native desktop](docs/NATIVE-DESKTOP.md),
  and [browser tools](docs/BROWSER.md)
- [Features](docs/FEATURES.md) and [capability matrix](docs/CAPABILITIES.md)

**Project**

- [Roadmap](docs/ROADMAP.md)
- [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md)
- [Phone app](docs/MOBILE.md)
- [Contributing](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md)

## Support

- Join the [Open Duet Discord community](https://discord.com/invite/zpnuBRXhKg)
  for questions and discussion.
- Report bugs and request features in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/Anil-matcha/open-duet/issues).
- For hosted account or billing questions, use the contact link on
  [suparagent.ai](https://suparagent.ai/contact/).

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. Start with the
[contributing guide](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md).

To propose a third-party app for the in-app MCP Marketplace, add a Community
manifest under `marketplace/plugins/community/`, regenerate
`marketplace/catalog.json`, and submit both in a pull request. See the
[MCP Marketplace submission guide](marketplace/plugins/README.md) for the
manifest requirements and validation steps.
